sentences.text: Nadia asked Mr Petrov, in the end, what he thought the owl was doing.

He said that was the wrong question and that she should ask a better one, which annoyed her a great deal at the time and which she has since decided was the single most useful thing anybody said to her that year.
The better question took her until about February.
The better question was: *why does it only say the middle one?* Because it does.
Nobody in Block C has ever reported hearing their first name out of that window.
Nadia has now asked, over nine years, something like thirty people, and the answer has never varied.
It says the one that is not in use.
Which means — and this is the part she worked out on a landing in February with her hands in her sleeves, and which she has never had a better theory for since — that it is not identifying anybody.
If it wanted to identify her it would say Nadia.
Nadia is what she answers to; Nadia is on the buzzer and the register and the library card.
Saying the other one is, as an act of identification, useless.
It is doing the opposite thing.
It is saying the part that is not being used, to the one person who knows it is not being used, in an empty stairwell, at night, where nobody else can hear.
Mr Petrov, when she put this to him in the lift in March, listened to all of it and then said only: "Yes." "Yes what?" "Yes, that is what it is doing." The lift went past four.
"You wanted me to say whether it is a good thing.
I am not going to.

Mrs Deniz thinks it is not, and Mrs Deniz has buried two husbands and I have buried none, so I have stopped assuming I know." She told her mother in April, in the kitchen, and did not manage it well, and her mother did not cry, and they sat there for a while afterwards not saying much.
Nadia is Nadia at work.

She wants that clear, because people who hear this story sometimes want it to end with her changing everything back, and she did not, and she does not intend to, and she does not think that would have been braver.
What she did do, when she was nineteen, was write it — all three syllables, correctly, with the sound in the middle — on the inside cover of every notebook she owns, where nobody else looks.

And she lived in Block C until she was twenty-three, and for the last four of those years she went up to the fourth-floor landing perhaps once a month, at night, in the cold, and stood by the gap in the window until something on the ledge outside said it out loud in the right voice with the stress in the right place.
The window has been fixed now.

She has been back twice and it shuts perfectly, and she has heard nothing either time, and she is entirely at peace about this and has told the building's committee that they did the right thing, which was a lie.
